summaryEn: Taiwan's largest LED maker survived the commoditisation of visible light by moving into the light you cannot see — infrared and optical sensing is now 40% of revenue, automotive another 16%. It pays a 7.1% yield, and distributes almost everything it earns to do so.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + press; LED framing — the pivot to invisible light (40%) and automotive (16%), the escape from Chinese price competition and the Nichia patent outcomes credited with the expired patent stated, but FY2024's NT$6.64 EPS identified as flattered by a 2024Q4 non-operating gain, gross margin falling 30.4%→24.7%, the ~98% payout underpinning the 7.12% yield, and operating cash flow well below net profit all stated plainly; sector Optoelectronics → LED & Optoelectronic Components)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
Everlight Electronics (億光電子, TWSE: 2393) is Taiwan's largest LED packaging company, and its recent history is a study in what happens when a growth industry becomes a commodity. Founded in **1983** and **listed in November 1999**, it grew with the global shift from incandescent bulbs to solid-state lighting — and then watched Chinese producers, backed by vast subsidised capacity, turn visible-light LEDs into a business almost nobody makes money in. Chinese optoelectronics leaders have recorded **ten consecutive quarters of losses**.

Everlight's response was to move to where the price war is not. **Invisible light — infrared emitters, optical couplers and sensing components — is now about 40% of revenue**, sold into industrial control, programmable logic controllers, photovoltaic inverters, advanced power supplies and wearable sensing. **Automotive products are another 16%**, and are described by the company as a critical profit pillar with double-digit growth expected in 2026 as customer inventories normalise. The strategic logic is simple: components that are qualified into an industrial controller or a car are chosen on reliability and specification, not on price per lumen.

It also spent much of two decades in **patent litigation with Japan's Nichia**, the company whose white-LED patents defined the industry. Everlight has won favourable rulings in the **United States, Australia, China and Taiwan** challenging Nichia's YAG patents, and in the German case the compensation was reduced to **€1.63m (roughly NT$59.57m)**, with Everlight considering an appeal; the disputed patent **expired in July 2017**.

The financials show a business that is stable but not improving. Annual EPS ran **NT$2.79 (FY2022) → 3.32 → 6.64 (FY2024) → NT$4.60 (FY2025)**, though **FY2024's figure is flattered**: that year's fourth quarter posted a **19.4% net margin against an 8.0% operating margin**, meaning a large non-operating gain. More recently, **gross margin has fallen from 30.4% (2025Q1) to 24.7% (2026Q1)** and operating margin from **12.4% to 7.4%**, which the company attributes to rising raw-material prices; analysts doubt gross margin returns above 30% even with cost pass-through. **2026Q1 EPS was NT$0.91 against NT$1.32 a year earlier.**

What the shares offer is income. At **NT$63.20 they trade on 15.1× earnings and 1.36× book with a 7.12% dividend yield** — the highest in this collection — backed by a conservative **31.1% debt ratio** and **NT$5.02bn of cash**. But the FY2025 dividend of **NT$4.5 against EPS of NT$4.60 is a payout of roughly 98%**, and **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$136m fell well short of NT$416m of net profit**.

The honest read: **a genuine escape from a commodity trap into defensible niches — attached to a company paying out essentially all of its earnings while its margins compress.**

Everlight was founded in **1983**, when light-emitting diodes were indicator lamps — the small red dot on a stereo, the display of a calculator. Packaging them was precision assembly work: mounting a semiconductor die, wiring it, encapsulating it in resin so it emitted light reliably for years. Taiwan was good at exactly this kind of manufacturing, and Everlight became the island's largest LED packager. It **listed in 1999**.

Then the industry's defining event: **white LEDs**. Nichia of Japan developed the blue LED and the phosphor conversion that turned it white — the breakthrough that made solid-state lighting possible and later won a Nobel Prize. It also produced a patent estate that Nichia defended aggressively worldwide. Everlight, competing in general lighting, spent much of two decades **in litigation with Nichia** across multiple jurisdictions, and won favourable rulings challenging Nichia's YAG patents in the **United States, Australia, China and Taiwan**. In the German case the claimed compensation was ultimately reduced to **€1.63m**, and the disputed patent **expired in July 2017**.

But the more consequential threat was not legal. As LED lighting went mainstream, **Chinese producers built enormous subsidised capacity**, and visible-light LEDs became a commodity sold on price. Margins across the industry collapsed; Chinese optoelectronics leaders have since posted **ten consecutive quarters of losses**. A Taiwanese packager could not win that fight, and Everlight did not try to.

Instead it went where the light is invisible. **Infrared emitters and receivers, optical couplers and sensing components** are not sold by the lumen — they are designed into industrial controllers, power supplies, photovoltaic inverters, wearable devices and vehicles, where qualification takes time, reliability matters more than price, and Chinese volume production carries less advantage. Today **invisible light is about 40% of revenue and automotive a further 16%** — a company that survived by ceasing to compete in the market it grew up in.

- **1983 (28 May)** — Everlight Electronics founded to package light-emitting diodes.
- **1990s** — Becomes Taiwan's largest LED packager as LEDs move from indicators into displays and backlighting.
- **1999 (4 Nov)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (2393)**.
- **2000s–2010s** — The white-LED lighting boom, and **prolonged patent litigation with Nichia** across multiple jurisdictions; Everlight wins favourable rulings in the **US, Australia, China and Taiwan** on Nichia's YAG patents.
- **2010s** — **Chinese subsidised capacity commoditises visible-light LEDs**; industry margins collapse. Everlight begins shifting toward invisible light and automotive.
- **2017 (29 July)** — The patent disputed in the German Nichia case **expires**.
- **2022** — FY2022 EPS **NT$2.79**, including a small Q4 loss; dividend NT$2.5.
- **2023** — **EPS NT$3.32**; dividend **NT$3.2**.
- **2024** — Reported **EPS NT$6.64** — but **Q4 carried a 19.4% net margin against an 8.0% operating margin**, a large non-operating gain. Dividend raised to **NT$5.31**.
- **2025** — **EPS NT$4.60**; gross margin peaks at **32.1%** in Q2 then declines; dividend **NT$4.5** — roughly a **98% payout**.
- **2026Q1** — **EPS NT$0.91** (from NT$1.32); **gross margin 24.7%, operating margin 7.4%** on rising raw-material costs. **Invisible light ~40% of revenue, automotive ~16%.** German Nichia compensation reduced to **€1.63m**.

Everlight's accounts show **a stable, conservatively financed business paying out nearly everything it earns, while its margins compress**.

- **Earnings that rose and then gave part of it back.** Annual EPS: **NT$2.79 (FY2022) → 3.32 (FY2023) → 6.64 (FY2024) → NT$4.60 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 at NT$0.91 against NT$1.32** a year earlier. Trailing **return on equity is 8.93%**.
- **FY2024's figure needs a footnote.** That year's fourth quarter reported a **19.4% net margin against an 8.0% operating margin** — an eleven-point gap indicating a substantial **non-operating gain**. FY2024's headline **NT$6.64** therefore overstates the operating earning power of that year, and makes FY2025's NT$4.60 look like a bigger decline than the operations delivered.
- **Margins are compressing now.** Gross margin: **27.6% (2024Q4) → 30.4% → 32.1% → 31.5% → 30.2% → 24.7% (2026Q1)**. Operating margin: **12.4% (2025Q1) → 7.4% (2026Q1)**. The company attributes this to **rising raw-material prices**, and analysts covering it doubt gross margin returns above 30% even with cost pass-through to customers.
- **The dividend is the investment case, and it is stretched.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$1.4 (2019) → 2.25 → 3.5 → 2.5 → 3.2 (2023) → 5.31 (2024) → NT$4.5 (2025)**. Against FY2025 EPS of **NT$4.60**, that is a payout of roughly **98%** — essentially all earnings distributed. The **7.12% yield** at NT$63.20 is the highest in this collection, and it depends on earnings holding.
- **Cash flow below profit.** **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$136m** against **NT$416m of net income**. One quarter is not a trend, but with a near-100% payout the gap matters.
- **A genuinely conservative balance sheet.** **NT$30.7bn of assets** on **NT$21.1bn of equity** — a **31.1% debt ratio** — with **NT$5.02bn of cash**. This is the cushion that makes a high payout survivable.
- **Valuation.** **15.1× earnings, 1.36× book**. The market prices it as a mature, ex-growth income stock, which is a fair description.

The financing reality: **a well-capitalised company that has successfully repositioned its product mix, distributing almost all of its profit while the profit itself is under cost pressure.**

**Stance: a real escape from LED commoditisation into invisible light and automotive, paying a 7.12% yield — from a payout of roughly 98% of earnings, with gross margin falling.**

The bull case:

1. **The pivot worked, and is measurable.** **Invisible light is ~40% of revenue** — infrared, optical couplers and sensing designed into industrial controllers, PLCs, photovoltaic inverters, power supplies and wearables — and **automotive is ~16%**, with double-digit growth expected in 2026 as customer inventories normalise. These are specification-driven markets where Chinese volume pricing carries far less weight.
2. **The commodity fight is over and Everlight is not in it.** Chinese optoelectronics leaders have posted **ten consecutive quarters of losses** in visible-light LEDs. Everlight earns an **8.93% ROE** and a **31.1% debt ratio** by not competing there.
3. **Genuine income.** A **7.12% yield** at **1.36× book** and **15.1× earnings**, supported by **NT$5.02bn of cash**.
4. **Legal overhang largely resolved.** Favourable rulings against Nichia's YAG patents in the **US, Australia, China and Taiwan**; the German compensation reduced to **€1.63m** and the patent itself **expired in 2017**.

The counter-arguments:

- **The payout leaves no room.** **NT$4.5 distributed against NT$4.60 earned** is roughly **98%**. Any earnings decline forces a dividend cut, and the dividend is why most holders own it.
- **Margins are going the wrong way.** Gross margin **30.4% → 24.7%**, operating margin **12.4% → 7.4%**, on raw-material costs analysts do not expect to fully reverse.
- **FY2024's NT$6.64 was flattered** by a non-operating gain, so the earnings base is lower than the four-year series suggests.
- **Growth is modest.** Monthly revenue has ranged **−5% to +12%**; this is a repositioning story, not an expansion one.

An **income-with-a-caveat** thesis: a well-run survivor in defensible niches, bought for a yield that is only as safe as next year's margins.

Everlight packages semiconductor light sources and sensors, and its economics depend entirely on **which kind**:

- **Invisible light (~40% of revenue) — the profitable core.** Infrared emitters and receivers, **optical couplers** (which pass a signal between two circuits using light, providing electrical isolation), and sensing components. These go into **industrial control systems, programmable logic controllers, photovoltaic inverters, advanced power supplies and wearable devices**. They are selected on specification, reliability and long-term availability — designed into a product and rarely changed — which is why they hold margin.
- **Automotive (~16%) — the second pillar.** Interior and exterior lighting and sensing for vehicles. Automotive qualification is slow and demanding (temperature range, vibration, lifetime), so positions are durable once won, and content per vehicle rises with electrification and driver-assistance systems.
- **Visible-light LEDs — the legacy.** General lighting and display backlighting, where Chinese subsidised capacity turned the product into a commodity. This is the part of the business that the strategy has been steering away from.
- **What packaging actually involves.** Everlight buys or makes LED dies, then mounts, wires and encapsulates them into usable components. The value is in **thermal management, optical design, reliability engineering and qualification** — making a device that performs to specification for a decade inside a car or an industrial controller.
- **Why the mix determines the margin.** A general-lighting LED competes on price per lumen against unlimited capacity. An infrared sensing component qualified into a photovoltaic inverter competes on whether it works. That difference is the entire reason gross margin sits near 25–30% rather than in single digits.

The levers are **mix (invisible light and automotive share), raw-material costs, and design wins that lock in multi-year supply**. The strength is that the company has already made the transition — the high-margin segments are the majority. The vulnerability is that **it is a component packager, not a designer of end systems**: it takes raw-material cost increases directly, as **2026Q1's fall to a 24.7% gross margin** demonstrated, and can pass them on only slowly.

The LED industry is the clearest example in this collection of a technology boom that ended in commoditisation.

- **What happened.** Solid-state lighting was one of the great efficiency transitions — LEDs replaced incandescent and fluorescent lighting worldwide within about fifteen years. That created a demand surge, which attracted enormous capacity, much of it **Chinese and subsidised**. Once installed, that capacity had to run, and prices fell until nobody earned a return. Chinese optoelectronics leaders have recorded **ten consecutive quarters of losses** — an industry producing at a loss because stopping is worse.
- **Where profit still exists.** Not in lumens, but in **function**. Infrared emitters for sensing, optical couplers for electrical isolation, and automotive-qualified devices are selected on performance and reliability, designed into systems, and requalified only reluctantly. Taiwanese LED makers as a group have pursued exactly this escape — **invisible light, automotive, low-temperature lighting and silicon photonics**.
- **The patent dimension.** **Nichia** of Japan created the white LED and defended its patents globally for two decades. Everlight was among its most persistent opponents, winning favourable rulings in the **US, Australia, China and Taiwan** on Nichia's YAG patents. With the German patent **expired since July 2017** and compensation reduced to **€1.63m**, this historical overhang is largely behind the company.
- **The automotive opening.** Vehicles use more optoelectronics every generation — lighting, cabin sensing, driver monitoring, proximity detection — and automotive qualification is a barrier that favours established suppliers. This is the same qualification-driven dynamic that protects Elite Material and King Yuan Electronics elsewhere in this collection.
- **The remaining pressure.** Everlight buys raw materials in a market it does not control, and sells components into customers who resist price increases. **Gross margin fell from 30.4% to 24.7% in four quarters** on exactly that squeeze.

Everlight's position is **defensible in the segments it has moved into and irrelevant in the one it left**. The industry truth is that **escaping a commodity trap changes what you sell, not whether your customers will pay more when your costs rise.**

**Strengths**
- **Successful mix shift**: invisible light **~40%** of revenue (industrial control, PLCs, PV inverters, optical couplers, wearable sensing), automotive **~16%**.
- **Conservative balance sheet**: **31.1% debt ratio**, **NT$5.02bn cash**, **NT$21.1bn equity**.
- **Nichia patent overhang largely resolved** — favourable rulings in the US, Australia, China and Taiwan; German compensation cut to **€1.63m**; patent expired 2017.
- **7.12% dividend yield** at **1.36× book** and **15.1× earnings**.

**Weaknesses**
- **Payout of roughly 98%** of FY2025 earnings — no retained cushion.
- **Gross margin falling 30.4% → 24.7%**, operating margin **12.4% → 7.4%**, on raw-material costs.
- **FY2024's NT$6.64 EPS flattered** by a Q4 non-operating gain (19.4% net margin vs 8.0% operating).
- **2026Q1 operating cash flow NT$136m** against NT$416m of net profit.

**Opportunities**
- Automotive content growth with electrification and driver-assistance systems.
- Photovoltaic inverters, industrial automation and wearable sensing expanding invisible-light demand.
- Chinese competitors' sustained losses eventually forcing capacity closures.

**Threats**
- **Continued raw-material inflation** compressing margin further.
- Chinese producers moving up into invisible light and automotive.
- **Dividend cut risk** if earnings decline from an already near-total payout.

- **The dividend has no cushion (the most immediate risk for income holders).** FY2025 distributed **NT$4.5 against EPS of NT$4.60 — roughly a 98% payout**. The **7.12% yield** is the primary reason to own the shares, and it is fully dependent on earnings not falling. **2026Q1 EPS of NT$0.91 was down from NT$1.32**, and **operating cash flow of NT$136m fell well short of NT$416m of net profit**.
- **Margins are compressing.** **Gross margin fell from 30.4% to 24.7%** and operating margin from **12.4% to 7.4%** across four quarters, on raw-material costs. Analysts covering the company doubt gross margin returns above 30% even with pass-through. As a component packager, Everlight absorbs input costs before it can recover them.
- **The earnings base is lower than it appears.** **FY2024's NT$6.64** included a substantial **non-operating gain** — that quarter's net margin was **19.4% against an 8.0% operating margin**. Comparisons against FY2024 overstate the decline; comparisons using FY2024 as a normal base overstate the company's earning power.
- **Chinese competitors are moving up.** The commodity segment Everlight left is loss-making for its Chinese rivals — which gives them every incentive to pursue the higher-margin invisible-light and automotive segments Everlight has retreated into.
- **Modest growth.** Monthly revenue has ranged **−5% to +12%** year-on-year. This is a repositioned mature business, not a growing one, and the valuation of **15.1× earnings** should be read accordingly.
- **Automotive cyclicality.** The 16% automotive segment depends on vehicle production and customer inventory cycles, which have already caused one destocking pause.

Everlight's outlook rests on **whether the high-margin mix can outrun input costs, and whether the dividend survives if it cannot.** The axes to watch:

- **Gross margin.** The decisive line. It has fallen **30.4% → 24.7%** in four quarters on raw materials, and the company is passing costs through. Recovery toward 30% would confirm pricing power in the niches; continued erosion would question it — and would put the dividend in play.
- **Invisible light and automotive share.** Currently **~40% and ~16%**. Both are expected to grow, automotive at double digits in 2026 as customer inventories normalise. A rising share of these segments is the structural driver of margin.
- **The payout.** **NT$4.5 against NT$4.60 earned.** Whether the board sustains that level through a margin squeeze — and whether operating cash flow recovers to support it — is the single most important question for anyone holding this for the **7.12% yield**.
- **Operating cash flow.** **NT$136m against NT$416m of net profit in 2026Q1.** With a near-total payout, cash conversion is not a technicality.

Bottom line: Everlight **escaped the commoditisation of LEDs** — the industry that made it and then destroyed its economics — by moving into **invisible light (~40% of revenue) and automotive (~16%)**, resolving a two-decade patent conflict with Nichia along the way, and now earns **8.93% on equity** with a **31.1% debt ratio** and **NT$5.02bn of cash**. It also pays out **roughly 98% of its earnings** to fund a **7.12% yield** while **gross margin has fallen from 30.4% to 24.7%** and **FY2024's headline EPS was flattered by a non-operating gain**. Judge it on **gross margin and cash conversion** — a successful repositioning whose income depends on holding the line on costs.
